A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL), with matching authors, framework, and core experiments. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison. The earlier prompting appendix can be matched to its expanded replacement in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original ARC few-shot learning and SQuAD knowledge-incorporation experiments, including prompting analyses and sequential-edit forgetting results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds larger-scale continued pretraining, additional comparators, model-size analysis, and reward and prompting experiments.

M1.justification: The main SEAL algorithm remains unchanged. Appendix B.10 introduces an alternative training procedure that replaces the adaptation-and-evaluation reward loop with summed GPT-4.1 rubric scores for length, diversity, quality, and correctness. This is a substantive but bounded reward variant.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ARC few-shot reasoning and knowledge incorporation using SQuAD v1.1 without passages in context. Expanding SQuAD evaluation from 200 to 2,067 passages changes sample coverage within the retained dataset and task, rather than introducing a new domain or task.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons with Generative Adapter and Entigraph, including entity-pair and pair-plus-triplet variants, in Tables 7–8. Table 10 also extends GPT-4.1-generated-data comparisons across prompting formats; v1's corresponding prompting table contained no such comparator column. The original main-table comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 and Table 2 now report full finetuning for continued pretraining, replacing the LoRA setting documented in v1, and add the full 2,067-passage validation set. New experiments introduce Qwen2.5-3B, a Mistral-7B-based Generative Adapter comparator, and additional prompting and reward protocols. However, v2's retained Table 4 still lists LoRA parameters, leaving the CPT settings incompletely reconciled.

E4.justification: v2 adds model-size sensitivity analysis and an ablation testing whether a cheap rubric reward can replace the costly inner loop. The prompting analysis, moved from Appendix C to B.11, gains no-prompt and chain-of-thought controls. These examine capacity dependence, reward necessity, and reliance on explicit prompting; the forgetting analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Section B.2 retains three-seed averaging when scoring self-edits during ReSTEM training. The catastrophic-forgetting SEM table is unchanged. The added experiments introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice, significance test, or stated increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces the 200-passage CPT results: SEAL/GPT-4.1 synthetic-data accuracy changes from 43.8/39.4 to 58.2/59.4 under the newly reported full-finetuning setting, reversing their ranking. The new 2,067-passage results are 46.4/49.2. Additional tables report comparator, model-size, and proxy-reward outcomes, including 45.6% for proxy reward versus 47.0% for full SEAL. The retained implications-long Round 2 entry changes from 51.8 to 54.4. These are not collectively same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The formal task/state definitions, RL objective, binary reward formulation, and stop-gradient derivation in Section 3.1 and Equations 1–4 are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical revision is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: learning to generate self-edit data and adaptation directives through RL. The introductory single-passage improvement and few-shot adaptation claims remain unchanged. Revised CPT rankings and appendix findings do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: v1 interprets lower CPT accuracy through possible gradient interference; v2 attributes higher CPT accuracy to aggregating generations and acknowledges GPT-4.1's lead. New discussion addresses proxy-reward cost versus direct adaptation feedback, unsuccessful format discovery without prompting, competitive structured heuristics, and possible capacity-dependent benefits with explicit scaling caveats. These substantially refine the method's interpretation and boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds the Generative Adapter backbone, Entigraph generation counts, proxy-grading categories and score scale, training-time comparison, and new prompt templates. Existing hardware, software, access information, and most hyperparameter documentation remain. Reproducibility is limited by the unreconciled LoRA table despite the new full-finetuning CPT description.

R1.justification: Related work expands with references including Generative Adapter, DataRater, Nemotron-CC, and RL's Razor. Transformer-Squared receives a more explicit explanation, and the appendices discuss SEAL's relationship to hypernetwork adaptation and structured synthetic-data generation. Entigraph's underlying work was already cited in v1; the overall research positioning remains.

P1.justification: The main section order and most prose remain intact. Changes include localized introduction, related-work, and results rewrites, updated conference text, and moving Prompting from Appendix C to B.11 alongside new appendix subsections. This is not an extensive narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adds four result tables, expands Table 2 with another CPT column and explicit adaptation labels, and transposes and expands v1's prompting Table 6 into Table 10. These substantially extend the tabular presentation. Figures 1–6 and the overall page design are largely retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny through direct alternative-method comparisons and tests of reward-loop necessity and dependence on prescribed prompting. Reporting cases where competitors outperform SEAL gives readers better-supported boundaries than v1 provided. The gains outweigh reporting weaknesses: Table 4 still documents LoRA despite full-finetuning CPT, and Tables 7 and 9 give a 32.0 base accuracy inconsistent with 32.7 elsewhere. These limit reproducibility but do not erase the value of the added critical evidence.
